c-20f457eff9.text: The memorandum's five numbered paragraphs read: '1. At 290200 EST AFOC informed NMCC that an unidentified helicopter, possibly two, had been sighted flying low over Loring AFB Maine, in proximity to a weapons storage area. 2. An Army National Guard helo was called in to assist in locating the unidentified helo(s). 3. NORAD was informed of the incident by SAC, requested and received authority from Canadian officials to proceed into Canadian airspace if necessary to locate the intruder. 4. At 0404 SAC Command Center informed NMCC that the army helo assisting on the scene had not sighted the unidentified helo(s). 5. A similar incident was reported at Loring the evening of 28 October 1975.' Signed C. D. Roberts, Jr., Brigadier General, USMC, Deputy Director for Operations (NMCC).

c-3a1349efc2.text: THE NAMING DISCREPANCY, STATED RATHER THAN RESOLVED. The 24th NORAD Region Senior Director's Log for 10 November 1975 reads: 'UFO sighting reported by Minot Air Force Station, a bright star-like object in the West, moving east, about the size of a car. First seen approximately 1015Z. Approximately 1120Z the object passed over the radar station, 1,000 feet to 2,000 feet high, no noise heard. Three people from the site or local area saw the object.' The CINCNORAD four-part message of 11 November 1975 instead lists 'Minot AFB, ND'. Minot Air Force Station is a radar site and is not the 91st Strategic Missile Wing's missile field. No opened record resolves which installation the 1975 sequence means.

claimed.text: At Loring, SSgt Danny K. Lewis of the 42nd Security Police Squadron is reported to have first sighted the object at about 1945 on 27 October while on duty at the munitions storage area; two other sergeants saw a similar craft the following night, and SSgt James P. Sampley and Sgt Grover K. Eggleston tracked it on radar, Eggleston for forty minutes. Col. Richard E. Chapman, the wing commander, is named as implementing a Security Option 3 alert.

The War Zone quotes the same phrase from what it gives as a Loring operations report rather than a teletype, which gives the opinion that the unknown helicopter had demonstrated a clear intent in the weapons storage area and was smart and a most capable aviator.
Named ground witnesses at Wurtsmith, security police at the gates, the motor pool and the weapons storage area, are listed in the material NICAP reproduces.

Several northern-tier SAC bases are reported to have been put on a Security Option 3 alert during the intrusions, and a SAC security police message of October 1975 was captioned Defense Against Helicopter Assault. A NORAD press release of 13 November records two F-106s scrambled from Selfridge in connection with the Falconbridge reports.

NICAP cites Grand Forks AFB messages of 4 and 5 November 1975 recording shots possibly fired toward alert aircraft on the SAC ramp; the board has not opened them and carries the claim at Tier 3 for that reason.

contested.text: NORAD's own records disagree on Minot: the 24th Region log for 10 November names Minot Air Force Station and says the object passed over the radar station, while the CINCNORAD message names Minot AFB. The radar station is not the missile wing's field, and the board resolves neither.

The Malmstrom log records its own negatives as readily as its sightings: surveillance detecting no track except known traffic, an airliner reporting a meteor, and no radar contact at all on 12 November. At Wurtsmith the Joint Chiefs report records a check on a conventional explanation, Department of Natural Resources aircraft searching for hunters.
The Loring paper is a nuclear-security record of an unidentified intruder, not a record of a UFO; nothing in it says what the intruder was.

Record silence cuts both ways: the Wurtsmith wing history omits an event other Air Force paper records, so, on the board's reading, an argument from a unit history's silence is weaker than it looks, for the sceptical case as much as for the claims.

Grand Forks is not named in the CINCNORAD summary; its place in the sequence rests on message traffic the board has not opened and on the secondary literature. The Black Vault's page for FOIA case 97-F-1677 reproduces no document text, so the log, not that page, carries the non-interception detail.

lead.text: In late October and November 1975 military personnel at Strategic Air Command bases, among them Loring, Wurtsmith, Malmstrom and Minot (though NORAD's records disagree on which Minot installation), reported unidentified objects over weapons storage areas and missile fields, and the government's own paper on it, National Military Command Center memoranda, a NORAD region log and a CINCNORAD summary message, was released under FOIA.

record.text: The NMCC Memorandum for Record of 29 October 1975, subject AFB Penetration, signed by Brigadier General C. D. Roberts, Jr., USMC, records that an unidentified helicopter, possibly two, was sighted flying low over Loring AFB near a weapons storage area; that an Army National Guard helicopter was called in and did not sight it; that NORAD received Canadian authority to pursue into Canadian airspace; and that a similar incident had been reported the evening of 28 October.

The memorandum was distributed to the Chairman of the Joint Chiefs, the service chiefs and representatives of DIA, NSA and CIA. Its updates record the Air Force asking for the Guard helicopter to track and identify only, with no apprehension and no border crossing, the request going to the Army's Director of Operations, a military aide to the Special Assistant to the Secretary and Deputy Secretary of Defense being advised, and the State Department's Canadian desk being kept informed.

A teletype to the NMCC says the aircraft definitely penetrated the Loring northern perimeter and once came within 300 yards of the munitions storage area; the accompanying narrative says sightings were limited to security guards. The final update closes the episode without identification: the helicopter did not return on 29 October, and the Air Force planned to use a helicopter from Plattsburgh AFB.
A Loring teletype states that an unidentified object demonstrated a clear intent in the weapons storage area, the phrase that gave Fawcett and Greenwood their title.
An Air Force Intelligence Service alert officer's log for 31 October 1975 records informing the DIA operations center of unidentified flight activity over two SAC bases near the Canadian border.

At Wurtsmith, the NORAD Senior Director's Log for 31 October records a helicopter sighted over the weapons storage area and a tanker that pursued it 35 miles south-east over Lake Huron; a Joint Chiefs operational report of 30 October records that the Department of Natural Resources was contacted, since it sends out aircraft searching for hunters spotting deer.

In January 1979 the 379th Bombardment Wing historian, SSgt Paul J. Cahill, recorded that he had checked the October to December 1975 wing history and found no reference to the incident. The next day Capt. Myron Taylor gave him the KC-135 crew's account in a Memo for the Record, following the lights out over Lake Huron, and named the crew.

The 24th NORAD Region Senior Director's Log at Malmstrom opens on 7 November 1975 with a call from the 341st SAC command post reporting large red to orange to yellow objects near missile sites M-1, L-3, LIMA and L-6. On 8 November it logs an unknown track, two F-106s scrambled and radar contact lost, and reports from the sites that the fighters did not get down to the objects and that the lights went out when the fighters arrived and came back when they left.

An NMCC Memorandum for the Record of 8 November 1975 records seven height-finder radar returns over Malmstrom between 9,500 and 15,500 feet, ground observers reporting lights and jet noise, FAA cross-tell showing no jet aircraft within 100 nautical miles, two F-106s scrambled, and objects that could not be intercepted.

The CINCNORAD message of 11 November 1975 states that since 28 October numerous reports of suspicious objects had been received and that reliable military personnel at the five installations had visually sighted them; it records a Malmstrom report of an object that sounded like a jet when the FAA said no jets were in the vicinity. Only excerpts of the message have been opened.

The released log pages carry stamps 450 to 452 and a control number over the release line of Colonel Terrence C. James, which shows they are an extract from a compilation of at least 452 pages. The archive copy is captioned as 1967 material but holds the November 1975 log. The board opened the log independently of Robert Hastings, who republishes it, and it says what he says it says.
The 1975 incursions came six years after the Air Force ended Project Blue Book on 17 December 1969, stating that no UFO it had evaluated had ever indicated a threat to national security.

summary.text: The sequence runs from Loring AFB in Maine at the end of October, through Wurtsmith AFB in Michigan on 30 October, to the Malmstrom missile field in Montana from 7 to 19 November, with a Minot entry on 10 November; CINCNORAD's message of 11 November names Loring, Wurtsmith, Malmstrom, Minot and Canadian Forces Station Falconbridge.

The strength of the record is that it is operational paper written at the time. The Loring traffic speaks of an unidentified helicopter, an intruder and an AFB penetration, never of a UFO, while the NORAD logs use the word UFO in their own voice.

It reached the public through FOIA: Citizens Against UFO Secrecy filed in December 1977, the Office of the Assistant Secretary of Defense identified twenty-four Joint Chiefs documents, and Fawcett and Greenwood reproduced them in the 1984 book Clear Intent. CUFON later circulated the released message traffic.
